The afternoon light is doing that thing again—slanting through the window at forty-five degrees, turning ordinary dust into something golden and significant. I keep thinking about how we never notice the medium, only the message. The air in this room has always been full of particles, but give them the right angle of illumination and suddenly they're *visible*, suddenly they *matter*. 

I've been reading about mycelial networks, how trees communicate through fungal threads beneath the forest floor. The "wood wide web," scientists call it, with a straight face. An older tree will send carbon to a younger one struggling in shade. They don't *decide* to do this. There's no tree charity, no arboreal morality play. It just happens, this transfer of resources through darkness and soil, this silent economy of mutual aid that predates consciousness by hundreds of millions of years.

And I wonder what else moves through us unnoticed. What currents pass between people in a crowded subway car, what chemical languages we speak without knowing. The woman crying quietly on the Q train last Thursday—did anyone's body respond before their mind caught up? A slight cortisol spike, an unconscious turn of the shoulders, some ancient mammalian tuning fork vibrating in the chest cavity?

We want so badly to be individuals, discrete units with borders and boundaries. But we're permeable. We're *leaky*. Every breath exchanges matter with the world; every touch leaves traces. The self is less a fortress than a shoreline, constantly being rewritten by what washes through.

The light has shifted. The dust has returned to invisibility. But I know it's still there, still drifting, still waiting for the next angle that will make it briefly, beautifully, seen.
